title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
question: If the universe is infinite and full of stars, why isn't the night sky blazing with light?
summary: A simple observation — the sky is dark at night — turns out to be one of the most revealing puzzles in cosmology, ruling out an infinite, static, eternal universe long before anyone had direct evidence of the Big Bang.
content:
The naive argument for a bright sky

Suppose the universe is infinite, eternal, and roughly uniformly filled with stars. Pick any direction and look. Your line of sight will eventually hit a star's surface, because in an infinite universe every line eventually terminates on something. A star farther away looks dimmer per unit area, but there are also more stars at that distance covering more of the sky, and the two effects cancel exactly: each patch of sky, no matter how small, should show the surface brightness of a star. The whole sky should look like the surface of the sun. Heinrich Olbers formalized this in 1823, though Kepler had wondered about it two centuries earlier and used the dark sky as evidence the universe must be finite.

Why the naive answer fails

The most common casual explanation — "space is mostly empty, so most sightlines miss stars" — doesn't actually resolve the paradox in an infinite universe; given infinite depth, sightlines are guaranteed to hit something eventually, even if hits are rare per unit distance. Dust absorbing starlight doesn't save the argument either, because dust would heat up and re-radiate the absorbed energy until it too glowed as brightly as the stars behind it, given infinite time for equilibrium. The paradox is genuinely a challenge to the premises, not a computational error.

What actually resolves it

The real universe breaks the premises in at least two independent ways. First, it has a finite age (about 13.8 billion years), so light from stars farther than about 13.8 billion light-years hasn't had time to reach us — there is a cosmic horizon. Second, the universe is expanding, so light from very distant, receding sources is redshifted out of the visible spectrum and diluted in energy, weakening its contribution. Even a finite but static universe with a horizon would already dodge the paradox: only finitely many stars are visible, so their combined light needn't saturate the sky. The expansion adds a second, independent dimming effect on top of that. Both point to the same conclusion Olbers' reasoning was implicitly testing: a sky this dark is incompatible with an infinite, static, eternal distribution of light sources.

A paradox that did real cosmological work

What makes this interesting isn't the resolution alone but what the paradox demonstrates about how physics finds hidden assumptions. A dark sky is such an unremarkable, everyday fact that it seems to carry no information. Yet treated rigorously, it rules out entire classes of cosmological models. This is a recurring pattern in physics: mundane observations, pushed hard enough with clean logic, become tests of the largest-scale structure of reality. The cosmic microwave background — the actual observed afterglow of the early universe — is in some sense the modern descendant of this question: it's what you get when you trace the sky's brightness back as far as light can travel, and what you find is not infinite starlight but a nearly uniform glow from the hot, young universe itself, redshifted down into microwaves.

perspectives.title: Historical Perspective
perspectives.description: Kepler used the dark sky in 1610 as an argument for a finite universe, decades before Newtonian gravity or any expansion data existed — a case of a simple observation constraining cosmology well ahead of the physics needed to fully explain it.

perspectives.title: Physics Perspective
perspectives.description: The resolution rests on two independent, non-negotiable facts: the universe has a finite age (so there's a light-travel-time horizon) and it's expanding (so distant light is redshifted and diluted). Either alone would soften the paradox; together they fully resolve it.

perspectives.title: Cosmological Perspective
perspectives.description: The cosmic microwave background is the empirical answer to 'how far back does the light actually go': not infinitely, but to a hot, opaque wall about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, beyond which the early universe was too dense for light to travel freely.

perspectives.title: Epistemological Perspective
perspectives.description: Olbers' paradox is a model case of theory-laden observation: 'the sky is dark' looks like a trivial datum, but combined with logical rigor about infinite sums, it becomes a falsification test for whole families of cosmological models.
